books.section: Topic 2.5 Interactions Between American Indians and Europeans

options.misconception: The towns were not military training camps; they were missionary villages.
options.text: To train Native peoples as soldiers for the English militia

options.misconception: The towns were not a gift of unwanted land; they were a program of conversion.
options.text: To give Native peoples land the English did not want
To convert Native peoples to Christianity and remake them as English

rationales.A: The towns were not military training camps; they were missionary villages.
rationales.B: The towns were not a gift of unwanted land; they were a program of conversion.
rationales.C: The passage is direct: praying towns were villages where Native converts lived under English law, dressed in European clothing, and were expected to give up their own customs. Conversion was only the first step — the towns were meant to remake Native peoples into English Christians, in dress, law, and daily life. The Puritans did not want converts who kept their old ways; they wanted new Englishmen.
rationales.D: French fur traders operated far to the north; the praying towns faced no French threat.
rationales.general:
1. Read what the towns required. English law, European clothing, and the abandonment of Native customs.
2. Ask what conversion meant here. It was not only a change of belief — it was a change of life.
3. Name the purpose. The Puritans wanted converts remade as Englishmen, not converts who kept their old ways.
Remember: when a mission demands a new way of life, not just a new belief, its aim is remaking, not only converting.

stem: According to the passage, what was the purpose of the praying towns in Massachusetts Bay?

stimulus.source_note: Original secondary passage written for this question, summarizing standard background on the praying towns and French missions.
stimulus.text: In Massachusetts Bay, Puritan ministers built “praying towns” — villages where Native converts lived under English law, dressed in European clothing, and were expected to give up their own customs. By the 1670s there were fourteen such towns. Yet even converted Native peoples remained second-class citizens in English eyes: they were judged by how completely they had abandoned their old ways. French Jesuit missionaries took the opposite approach, living among Native peoples and accepting that Christianity could blend with Native traditions.
